title: Prompt Engineering
note: A practitioner’s whitepaper written around Gemini on Vertex AI, with each technique shown as a filled-in prompt table (goal, model, temperature, top-K/top-P, prompt, output). Summaries are in our own words; the text stays in the PDF.
summary: Prompting is treated as an engineering loop: pick a model, set the sampling configuration, choose a technique, and record every attempt. The paper first explains the output controls (length, temperature, top-K, top-P) and how they interact, including the repetition loops that extreme settings cause. It then walks through the standard techniques, from zero- and few-shot through system, contextual and role prompts, step-back prompting, chain of thought, self-consistency, tree of thoughts, ReAct, automatic prompt engineering and prompts for writing, explaining, translating and debugging code. The last part is a list of habits: give examples, keep it simple, say what you want rather than what you don’t, use variables, structured output and schemas, and document attempts in a standard template.

chapters.title: Introduction and output configuration

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Anyone can write a prompt, but getting reliable output depends on wording, examples, structure and model settings together.

sections.title: Prompt engineering
sections.summary: Prompt engineering is iterative design of the input so the model predicts the output you want; it works best with direct access to model settings.

sections.title: Output length
sections.summary: Limiting output tokens only cuts generation off; it doesn’t make the model concise, so the prompt must ask for brevity too.

sections.title: Sampling controls
sections.summary: Temperature, top-K and top-P each restrict which tokens can be sampled, and they combine; the paper gives starting values and warns that very low or very high settings cause repetition loops.

chapters.summary: What a prompt is, why the paper uses the API rather than the chat app, and the sampling settings that shape every output.

chapters.title: Prompting techniques

sections.title: General prompting / zero shot
sections.summary: A plain instruction with no examples; works for simple tasks and is the baseline.

sections.title: One-shot & few-shot
sections.summary: One or a few examples show the format and the pattern; the examples should be varied and high quality.

sections.title: System, contextual and role prompting
sections.summary: System prompts set the task and output format, contextual prompts give background, role prompts give a voice; JSON output is recommended for structure.

sections.title: Step-back prompting
sections.summary: First ask a broader question, then feed its answer into the specific task, to bring relevant background into play.

sections.title: Chain of Thought (CoT)
sections.summary: Asking for step-by-step reasoning improves answers on reasoning tasks, especially combined with few-shot examples; it costs more tokens.

sections.title: Self-consistency
sections.summary: Sample several reasoning paths at higher temperature and take the majority answer.

sections.title: Tree of Thoughts (ToT)
sections.summary: Explore a tree of intermediate thoughts rather than a single chain, for problems that need search.

sections.title: ReAct (reason & act)
sections.summary: Interleave reasoning with tool calls (for example, search), observing results before the next step.

sections.title: Automatic Prompt Engineering
sections.summary: Use a model to generate candidate prompts, score them, and keep the best.

sections.title: Code prompting
sections.summary: Prompts for writing, explaining, translating and debugging code, with the caution that generated code must be read and tested.

chapters.summary: The main prompting techniques, each with a worked prompt and its configuration.

chapters.title: Best Practices

sections.title: Provide examples
sections.summary: Examples are the most effective single tool.

sections.title: Design with simplicity
sections.summary: Short, clear prompts with action verbs work better than complex ones.

sections.title: Be specific about the output
sections.summary: State the desired output precisely.

sections.title: Use Instructions over Constraints
sections.summary: Positive instructions tend to work better than lists of prohibitions.

sections.title: Control the max token length
sections.summary: Cap output length in the configuration or ask for it in the prompt.

sections.title: Use variables in prompts
sections.summary: Variables make prompts reusable across inputs.

sections.title: Experiment with input formats and writing styles
sections.summary: Wording, style and prompt type all change results, so try variants.

sections.title: For few-shot prompting with classification tasks, mix up the classes
sections.summary: In few-shot classification, shuffle the order of classes so the model doesn’t learn the order.

sections.title: Adapt to model updates
sections.summary: Retest prompts when the model changes.

sections.title: Experiment with output formats
sections.summary: Structured formats like JSON reduce hallucination and make output parseable.

sections.title: JSON Repair
sections.summary: JSON is verbose and can be cut off; repair libraries fix truncated output.

sections.title: Working with Schemas
sections.summary: JSON Schemas can structure the input too, focusing the model on the relevant fields.

sections.title: Experiment together with other prompt engineers
sections.summary: Compare prompts written by several people.

sections.title: CoT Best practices
sections.summary: For chain of thought: put the answer after the reasoning, extract it separately, and use temperature 0.

sections.title: Document the various prompt attempts
sections.summary: Log every attempt (goal, model, settings, prompt, output) in a standard table so results can be compared.
